paras: The lynching of three Black men at Rolling Fork Creek took place in early June 1881 near Locksburg (also spelled Lockesburg), Sevier County, Arkansas, when armed white men hanged three unnamed men accused of robbing and murdering a farmer, R. F. Hall. The men were caught in a manhunt and hanged from trees at the ford where Hall had been killed, the last two on the night of Tuesday, June 7. Dispatches from Little Rock carried the story across the country under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Just Retribution."

According to the Little Rock reports, Hall, described as an old, wealthy and "eccentric" farmer rumored to carry large sums of money, set out to visit friends or relatives in a neighboring county. Finding Rolling Fork Creek swollen by recent rains, he hired three Black men to help him across. The three were accused of knocking him down, taking twenty-five or thirty cents from his pockets, strangling him and throwing the body, weighted with stones, into the creek. The body lodged in drift or a fallen tree downstream, where, by the wire account, a "colored man" saw and recognized it the next day.

Once the news spread, "a large body of white men" gathered at the ford and took up the trail, while the New Orleans Democrat's dispatch said that "an old negro gave a clew" to the accused, who had fled to the woods. The man the papers called the ringleader was captured first; the Chicago Tribune said he confessed and "begged piteously for life," while the Democrat dispatch said he admitted his part but claimed he had been drunk. He was taken back to the creek bank and hanged from the limb of a tree.

The other two men were found hiding in the woods and, according to the wire, "confessed all." The Tribune placed their capture at nightfall on Tuesday and the Democrat dispatch "many miles from the scene"; both said they were brought back to the creek and hanged, by midnight in the Tribune's account. They were hanged beside the first man at the ford.

No names of the three men or of any of the lynchers were printed, and the coverage shows no arrests, inquest or official inquiry. The Tribune's correspondent wrote that the affair had caused "a whirlwind of excitement" in the neighborhood but that "the action of Judge Lynch is universally approved," and the Democrat dispatch said it was "generally approved."

The first reports were Little Rock specials of June 8 in the Memphis Daily Appeal and the Chicago Tribune, followed by a longer press-wire account dated June 9 and 10. Between June 10 and June 17 that wire ran from Nevada, California, Wyoming and Washington Territory to Connecticut, often with garbled names such as "Looksburg," "Levier county" and "A. F. Hall." Other papers shortened it to a line in crime columns, among them the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Watertown Republican, which spelled the victim "Hull."

White papers presented the accusation and the confessions as established fact and the lynching as deserved punishment. The Tribune called the accused "darkeys" and "guilty wretches," the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headed its item "Work of Vigilants," and the Savannah Morning News ran the Democrat's dispatch as "Judge Lynch at Work." In Arkansas the Batesville Guard ran only a one-sentence notice that the men had been hanged by "an infuriated party of citizens." Weeks later, on July 24, the Seattle Daily Intelligencer retold the story as a tale of the killers' "mistakes," ending with mounted lynchers who "hanged them without trial."

Accounts differ on the pursuit: the wire said the first man was caught after a few hours and the others before dark, the Tribune and Democrat dispatches placed the last capture on Tuesday night, and the Seattle paragraph said the chase lasted three days. A Minnesota brief in the Warren Sheaf said only two of the men were lynched, against three in every fuller account, and the sum taken was printed as thirty cents in the wires but $1 in Seattle.

reader.title: Lynching of three Black men at Rolling Fork Creek, Sevier County, Arkansas
bases: Three Black men accused of robbing and murdering a white farmer were hunted down by armed white men and hanged at the creek where the killing took place (A1, A2, A7).

Every account says the three accused men were hanged by a 'band of armed men', a 'large body of white men' or a 'vigilance committee' with no trial or officer involved, as punishment for the alleged murder, which the papers called 'Judge Lynch' and 'Just Retribution' (A2, A6, A7, A16).

Separate Little Rock dispatches to the Memphis Appeal, the Chicago Tribune, the New Orleans Democrat and the press wire agree on the murder and the hanging of three men at the creek, though all come from Little Rock and none from a local witness (A1, A2, A7, A16).

accounts.gist: Hall was murdered by three men hired to ferry him; whites organized, captured them and hanged them to a tree at the scene.

accounts.label: Tribune / New Orleans Democrat dispatch
accounts.gist: The ringleader was caught, confessed (or pleaded drunkenness) and was hanged; the other two were overtaken Tuesday night far from the scene, brought back and hanged by midnight, and the lynching was approved locally.

accounts.label: Press wire (June 9-10)
accounts.gist: A large body of white men followed the trail; one man was caught after a few hours and hanged at the ford, and the other two were found in the woods before dark, confessed and were hanged beside him.

accounts.label: Seattle paragraph
accounts.gist: Mounted lynchers pursued the three for three days and hanged them without trial; only $1 had been found on the traveler.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran it as 'Speedy Justice' and 'Just Retribution', calling the accused 'darkeys' and 'guilty wretches' and reporting the lynching 'universally approved'.
The Savannah Morning News headed the New Orleans Democrat dispatch 'Judge Lynch at Work' and called the hanging 'swift retribution'.
Most other papers ran the wire or a one-line brief in crime columns ('Tragical Tales', 'Telegraphic Jottings'), stating the accusation as fact.

conflicts.note: The two-man version appears only in a Minnesota brief; all fuller accounts say three.
